Specific information for this practical exam
During the exam, the supervisor or other competent biologist (not the invigilator) should obtain the
results needed for the supervisor’s report by following the relevant steps in the question paper. The
results should be recorded in the supervisor’s report.
Organisation of the exam
Ɣ
All candidates must have access to the materials required for Question 1 throughout the whole
period of the exam.
Ɣ
Half of the candidates will have access to the microscope and slide for a maximum time of one
hour from the start of the exam. These candidates should start with Question 2. After one hour, or
sooner if candidates have finished Question 2, they should move on to Question 1.
Ɣ
For Question 2, two candidates are not permitted to share the same microscope and slide at the
same time.
Ɣ
The other candidates should start with Question 1. After one hour, these candidates should be
given access to the microscope and slide. They should then move on to Question 2 as soon as
they are ready.
Ɣ
Candidates will only have access to the microscope and slide for one hour. They should be
advised that they can answer any part of the exam paper not requiring the microscope and slide
throughout the whole period of the exam.
Ɣ
Access arrangements to microscopes and slides, including instructions on which question to start
with and timings, must be explained to candidates before the start of the exam.

Preparation of materials
Urea solutions, S and U, may be prepared the day before the exam. The containers should be
covered and put in a refrigerator overnight.
The soya beans for the urease solution, E, must be soaked the day before the exam. The soya
bean extract must be prepared on the day of the exam.
S, U and E should be at room temperature before the start of the exam.
Ɣ
E, soya bean extract (urease solution)
Put 100 g of dried soya beans into a large beaker with 300 cm3 distilled water. Leave covered
overnight. On the day of the exam, transfer the contents of the large beaker to a blender, add
100 cm3 distilled water and liquidise for 1 minute. Strain the liquidised soya beans through muslin
into a beaker.
Ɣ
S, 5.0% urea solution
Sprinkle 5.0 g of urea into 80 cm3 of warm distilled water. Mix well. Make up to 100 cm3 with
distilled water.
Ɣ
U, 3.0% urea solution
Sprinkle 3.0 g of urea into 80 cm3 of warm distilled water. Mix well. Make up to 100 cm3 with
distilled water.

BIOLOGY
Paper 9700/12
Multiple choice
Key messages
Candidates performed well on Questions 3, 5, 6, 7, 9, 11, 16, 23, 28 and 31.
Candidates performed less well on Questions 13, 14, 15, 18, 27, 30, 36, 37 and 38.
There was no clear pattern in terms of which topics were challenging. Many of the questions where
candidates performed less well required particularly careful reading of both the question, and the options.
Other challenging questions relied on interpreting graphical data.
Comments on specific questions
Question 13
x
Option C was a common incorrect answer.
x
Although option A and option C both show lowest water solubility for the region at the centre of the cell
surface membrane, only option A shows a sudden change to high water solubility at a fixed distance
away from the centre in the correct option. This reflects the hydrophobic nature of the fatty acid tails in
the centre of a phospholipid bilayer, and the hydrophilic nature of the phosphate heads.
Question 14
x
Option B was a common incorrect answer.
x
Option B contains familiar terms for the secondary structure of proteins, such as E-pleated sheets and
D-helices. E-pleated sheets are not coils of amino acids. Furthermore, the polypeptides in a quaternary
structure do not necessarily need to be different.
Question 15
x
Option B was a common incorrect answer.
x
Candidates who opted for B decided that statements 1 and 2 about ribozymes and enzymes were
correct. Statement 1 is incorrect because, for enzymes, it is the active site and substrate, rather than the
R-groups, that are complementary.
x
Statement 3 is also correct. To check the validity of this statement, candidates needed to consider that
there are only 4 different bases in a polynucleotide and 20 different amino acids in a polypeptide. This
will mean that for a polymer made up of the same number of monomers, there are many more possible
combinations in a polypeptide.
Question 18
x
Option B was a common incorrect answer.
x
Candidates selecting option B had not noted that region Q consists only of the fatty acid hydrocarbon
tails. It does not include the region of a phospholipid molecule where the fatty acid tails are joined to
glycerol.

x
All options were popular.
x
This question relied on an understanding that in eukaryotes, a primary transcript is modified by the
removal of introns and joining together of exons to form mRNA. This does not occur in bacteria. This

Statement 3 is incorrect because the genetic code is universal.
Question 30
x
Option A was a common incorrect answer.
x
Those candidates who opted for A, rather than the correct option, B, had misidentified the muscular and

Question 36
x
Option A and option B were common incorrect answers.
x
The roles of the substances involved in the transport of oxygen and carbon dioxide in blood are often
confused by candidates. Candidates who opted for A or B incorrectly thought that
carbaminohaemoglobin is found in blood plasma.
Question 37
x
Option D was a common incorrect answer.
x
Option D is incorrect because the rings of cartilage in the trachea are not complete.
Question 38
x

Preparation of materials
All the materials must be prepared on the day of the exam.
[MH]
Ɣ
H, 3.0% hydrogen peroxide solution
This is prepared by putting 50 cm3 of 6% (20 volume) hydrogen peroxide
solution [MH] into a beaker and adding 50 cm3 distilled water.
Note: This is intentionally named as 1.0% on the question paper for candidates.
[MH]
Ɣ
U, 1.5% hydrogen peroxide solution
This is prepared by putting 50 cm3 of 3.0% hydrogen peroxide solution [MH] into
a beaker and adding 50 cm3 distilled water.
Ɣ
P, plant extract solution
This is prepared by using approximately 40 g of peeled potato. Cut the potato
into small pieces and liquidise with 100 cm3 water. Strain the mixture through a
fine sieve or piece of muslin and retain the liquid plant extract.
The activity of the plant extract solution should be tested before the exam:
Ɣ
Cut a disc of filter paper using a hole punch.
Ɣ
Put the filter paper disc into the plant extract, P.
Ɣ
Put 5 cm3 depth of 3.0% hydrogen peroxide solution, H, in a small beaker or
large test-tube.
Ɣ
Remove the filter paper disc from P and drop it into the hydrogen peroxide
solution. Start timing when the disc reaches the bottom.
Ɣ
Note the time taken for the disc to return to the surface of the solution.
The time for the disc to return to the surface of the solution should be
between 4 and 15 seconds.
If the time is less than 4 seconds, decrease the concentration of the plant
extract by diluting with water.
If the time is more than 15 seconds, increase the mass of plant material
used to make the extract.

The time for the disc to return to the surface of the solution should be between 4 and
10 seconds.

solution by diluting with water.
If the time is more than 10 seconds, increase the mass of plant material used to
make the plant extract solution.

Preparation of materials
All the materials must be prepared on the day of the exam.
[MH]
Ɣ
H, 3.0% hydrogen peroxide solution
This is prepared by putting 50 cm3 of 6% (20 volume) hydrogen peroxide solution
[MH] into a beaker and adding 50 cm3 distilled water.
Note: This is intentionally named as 1.0% on the question paper for candidates.
Ɣ
P, plant extract solution
This is prepared by using approximately 40 g of peeled potato. Cut the potato into
small pieces and liquidise with 100 cm3 water. Strain the mixture through a fine sieve
or piece of muslin and retain the liquid plant extract.
The activity of the plant extract solution should be tested before the exam:
Ɣ
Cut a disc of filter paper using a hole punch.
Ɣ
Put the filter paper disc into the plant extract solution, P.
Ɣ
Put 5 cm depth of 3.0% hydrogen peroxide solution, H, in a small beaker or
large test-tube.
Ɣ
Remove the filter paper disc from P and drop it into the hydrogen peroxide solution.
Start timing when the disc reaches the bottom.
Ɣ
Note the time taken for the disc to return to the surface of the solution.
The time for the disc to return to the surface of the solution should be between 4 and
10 seconds.
If the time is less than 4 seconds, decrease the concentration of the plant extract
solution by diluting with water.
If the time is more than 10 seconds, increase the mass of plant material used to
make the plant extract solution.

allowances should not be used as a guide for teaching and learning.

Examiners award marks where it is clear that candidate responses have met the requirements of the mark
scheme. These requirements may vary between different components or different versions of the same
component, depending on the exact requirements of the question and the candidate responses seen during
the standardisation process.

specific question to support candidates and make sure that our assessments are fair. However, these
allowances should not be used as a guide for teaching and learning.

together with the assessment material and the Principal Examiner Report for Teachers.

This mark scheme contains the instructions and marking guidance that our examiners used to mark
candidate responses for this component.
Before they start marking, examiners complete a standardisation process. They review a range of candidate
responses and discuss the mark scheme in detail to agree which answers can and cannot be accepted.
Examiners award marks where it is clear that candidate responses have met the requirements of the mark
scheme. These requirements may vary between different components or different versions of the same
component, depending on the exact requirements of the question and the candidate responses seen during
the standardisation process.
Sometimes, our mark schemes may allow marks to be awarded to responses which contain elements that
are factually incorrect or for content not covered by the syllabus. We do this in response to the demands of a
specific question to support candidates and make sure that our assessments are fair. However, these
allowances should not be used as a guide for teaching and learning.
We cannot discuss the mark scheme with schools, and we recommend that schools read the mark scheme
together with the assessment material and the Principal Examiner Report for Teachers.

When potato pieces are soaked in methylene blue solution, the solution enters the potato tissue
and stains it blue.
When the potato pieces are placed in water, the blue colour moves out of the tissue into
the water.
You will investigate the effect of temperature on the movement of the blue colour out of the
potato tissue.
You are provided with the materials shown in Table 1.1.

Methylene blue solution can stain clothing and skin. Use blunt forceps to handle the potato
pieces and if any methylene blue comes into contact with your skin, wash it off immediately.
It is recommended that you wear suitable eye protection.

step 1
Remove the five potato pieces from the beaker labelled P and cut them into
lengths of 3 cm. Some methylene blue solution is released when the potato
pieces are cut.
step 2
Empty the coloured water from P into the container labelled For Waste.
step 3
Put the potato pieces back into P and cover them with tap water from the
beaker labelled T.
step 4
Stir the potato pieces with a glass rod.
step 5
Repeat step 2 to step 4 four more times. The water in P should now be pale
blue or colourless.
step 6
Set up a water-bath at 25 'C. The water-bath will be needed in step 11.
step 7
Remove the potato pieces from P and put them on a paper towel.
step 8
Label two test-tubes 25 'C.
step 9
Put one potato piece into one of the labelled test-tubes.
step 10
Put 10 cm3 of distilled water, W, into the test-tube with the potato piece.
step 11
Put this test-tube into the water-bath at 25 'C.
step 12
Start timing and leave the test-tube in the water-bath for 5 minutes.

step 13
After 5 minutes, remove the test-tube from the water-bath.

Stir the contents of the test-tube with a clean glass rod. Pour the water from this

piece in the first test-tube.

Repeat step 8 to step 16 until all the temperatures stated in 1(a)(i) have been
tested, finishing with the maximum temperature of 65 'C.

Observe the colour intensity of the water in each of the test-tubes in the
